claims: The Jones Act is the Merchant Marine Act of 1920.
The Jones Act is a federal statute.
The Jones Act requires that all goods transported by water between U.S. ports be carried on U.S.-flagged vessels.
The Jones Act requires that all goods transported by water between U.S. ports be carried on U.S.-built vessels.
The Jones Act requires that all goods transported by water between U.S. ports be carried on U.S.-owned vessels.
The Jones Act requires that vessels be manned by U.S. citizens.
Jones Act vessels must be built in the U.S.
Jones Act vessels must be owned by U.S. citizens.
Jones Act vessels must be crewed by at least 75% Americans.
The Jones Act governs maritime commerce between U.S. ports.
The Jones Act governs shipments to Hawaii.
The Jones Act governs shipments to Alaska.
The Jones Act governs shipments to Puerto Rico.
The Jones Act was enacted post-WWI.
The Jones Act provides a legal cause of action for sailors injured at sea due to negligence.
Critics argue the Jones Act limits competition, creating higher shipping costs which can increase prices for goods, particularly in Hawaii and Puerto Rico.
The Jones Act can be waived by the Department of Homeland Security if it is in the interest of national defense.
In March 2026, the Jones Act was temporarily waived.
The March 2026 Jones Act waiver allowed foreign-flagged vessels to move oil.
The March 2026 Jones Act waiver allowed foreign-flagged vessels to move natural gas.
The March 2026 Jones Act waiver allowed foreign-flagged vessels to move fuel.
The March 2026 Jones Act waiver was to help lower energy prices during the Iranian conflict
